extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, and students of English usage
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for correct and stylistically preferable English word choice, grammar constructions (e.g., cleft sentences), and common usage pitfalls for writers and editors producing Standard Written English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleft sentences (definition and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences beginning with an expletive it (the it-clause) plus a be-verb that emphasize new information identifying a person, place, time, object, cause, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'It was Manuel who met Adam in college.' Emphasis falls on the focused element in the cleft clause. The relative-pronoun clause often refers to already-given information and may be reduced when understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of cleft sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleft sentences may be declarative or interrogative, positive or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decl./Interrogative examples provided; negatives use simple negation (not, no). Relative pronoun often elided in whiz-deletion. Positive states a truth; negative states the contrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cleft sentences (stylistic guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cleft sentences can be used for dramatic effect to signal a shift, create an interesting lead-in, or imply contrast/mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'It was hours later that Burns discovered...' or 'It’s not Joan who wants to be a social activist' (implies contrast or mistaken identification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar versus usage (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many issues writers face are usage (collective habits of native speakers) rather than grammar; usage is descriptive and evolving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries describe how words are used but do not always prescribe standard print usage; consult usage/style guides (e.g., Fowler, Garner) for editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting dictionaries versus usage guides
rubrics_metrics.description: A word's presence in a dictionary doesn't guarantee fitness for Standard Written English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lexicographers document usage; editors should consult authoritative usage/style guides for prescriptive guidance and to resolve thorny points (e.g., infer vs imply).

rubrics_metrics.name: a; an (indefinite article use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a' before words beginning with a consonant sound and 'an' before words beginning with a vowel sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pronunciation (e.g., 'an hour-long talk' because h is silent). Initialisms pronounced as letters take 'an' (an HTML website) while acronyms pronounced as words may take 'a' (a NATO representative).

rubrics_metrics.name: ability; capability; capacity (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes the senses: ability = a person's power/skill; capability = general power or suitability for challenging tasks or features; capacity = container/amount or a person's potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the ability to ride a bicycle'; 'long-distance-flight capability'; 'a high-capacity fuel tank'; figurative and formal uses noted (capacity for love; in an advisory capacity).

rubrics_metrics.name: abjure; adjure (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abjure: to deny or renounce publicly; adjure: to charge or earnestly urge someone to do something (as if under oath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misusing adjure for abhor or require. Examples demonstrate proper usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: about; approximately (preferred contexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the adverb 'about' where idiomatically possible; in scientific contexts prefer 'approximately'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid coupling with another approximation word like 'guess' or 'estimate'. Example: 'approximately 32 coding-sequence differences'.

rubrics_metrics.name: abstruse
rubrics_metrics.description: Entry redirects to 'obtuse' (refers to meaning and usage cross-reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 'obtuse' for usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: accept; except (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept: to receive or regard as proper. Except: to exclude; 'to except to' means to object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'accept this gift' vs 'club members will be excepted from the admission charge'.

rubrics_metrics.name: access, verb (usage note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using nouns as verbs is common; 'access' as a verb is acceptable in computing contexts but can be jarring outside the digital world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable: 'access a computer', 'access the internet'; avoid non-digital uses when they sound awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: accord; accordance (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accord = agreement; accordance = conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'we are in accord', 'printed in accordance with modern industry standards'.

rubrics_metrics.name: acquiesce (preposition usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: To acquiesce means to allow or comply passively; traditionally takes 'in' though 'to' is accepted; 'with' is not standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the minority party acquiesced in the nomination.'

rubrics_metrics.name: actual fact, in (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In actual fact' is redundant; prefer 'actually' or omit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concision: 'Try actually instead, or simply omit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: acuity; acumen (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acuity = sharpness of perception (visual acuity); acumen = mental prowess/judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately: visual acuity vs business acumen.

rubrics_metrics.name: adduce; deduce; induce (meanings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adduce = cite as proof; deduce = reason from general to specific; induce = generalize from observations or mean to persuade/cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show logical vs common uses: 'adduced her four years...' ; 'deduce that the butler did it'; 'induce labor' or 'induce someone to do something.'

rubrics_metrics.name: adequate; sufficient; enough (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate = suitability in context; sufficient = amount enough to meet a need (with abstract/mass nouns/plurals); enough = everyday word modifying count or mass nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'adequate explanation'; 'sufficient water'; 'enough people'.

rubrics_metrics.name: adherence; adhesion (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adherence is figurative (devotion/observance); adhesion is mostly literal (sticking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'your adherence to the transportation code requires the adhesion of an inspection sticker.'

rubrics_metrics.name: adjure (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'abjure' (entry cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: administrator (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'executor' (entry cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: admission; admittance (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission is figurative (rights/privileges) or price; admittance is more literal physical entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the student won admission'; 'no admittance beyond this point.'

rubrics_metrics.name: adopted; adoptive (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopted applies to the child; adoptive describes the ones doing the adopting (adoptive parents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'adopted' to describe parents.

rubrics_metrics.name: adverse; averse (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverse = unfavorable or strongly opposed, typically refers to things; averse = feeling negatively about, refers to people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'adverse relations'; 'he's averse to asking for directions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: affect; effect (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affect is almost always a verb meaning to influence; effect is usually a noun meaning result but can be a verb meaning to bring about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note noun 'affect' in psychology for emotional expressiveness. Examples clarify use: 'the adverse publicity affected the election' vs 'the candidate’s attempted explanations had no effect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: affirmative/in the negative (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pompous ways to say 'yes' or 'no'; prefer ordinary 'he said yes' and 'she said no' without quotes or capitalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid elevated phrasing when plain wording suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: afflict (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'inflict' for usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: affront (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'effrontery' for usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: after having [+ past participle] (redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: This construction is often redundant; prefer 'after' + present participle or 'having' + past participle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change 'after having passed the audition, she...' to 'after passing the audition, she...' or 'having passed the audition, she...' See 5.110.

rubrics_metrics.name: afterward; afterword (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Afterward = adverb meaning 'later'; afterword = noun meaning 'epilogue'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also see 'afterwards' and 'toward' entries for related forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: aggravate (preferred sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally means to intensify something bad; avoid using it to mean 'to bother'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you mean 'to bother', prefer annoy, irritate, or exasperate. Examples: 'aggravate an injury.'

rubrics_metrics.name: aid; aide (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aid = noun (assistance) or verb (to help); aide = noun (helper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'teacher’s aide'; military 'general’s aide'.

rubrics_metrics.name: ain’t (register)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectal contraction; do not use except for nonstandard dialogue or jest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: alibi (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'alibi' as synonym for 'excuse'; traditional sense refers to defense of having been elsewhere when a crime was committed.

rubrics_metrics.name: all (of) (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete 'of' when possible ('all the houses', 'all my children'); exception when preceding nonpossessive pronoun ('all of us').

rubrics_metrics.name: alleged (usage trend)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally applied to acts (alleged burglary) rather than actors, but that distinction has largely been abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation note provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: all ready / already (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'already' entry: 'already' refers to time; 'all ready' refers to preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the movie has already started' vs 'are the actors all ready?'

rubrics_metrics.name: all right / alright (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words 'all right' is correct; 'alright' is traditionally nonstandard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'alright'.

rubrics_metrics.name: all together / altogether (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: All together refers to unity of time/place; altogether means wholly or entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the family will be all together' vs 'that story is altogether false.'

rubrics_metrics.name: allude; elude; illude (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allude = hint at; elude = avoid capture; illude (rare) = deceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often 'allude' is used loosely where 'refer' or 'quote' would be better.

rubrics_metrics.name: allusion; reference (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusion = indirect/casual mention; reference = direct/formal mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: literary allusion vs scholarly reference; see 'reference' entry for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: alongside (preposition usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning 'at the side of,' should not be followed by 'of'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'alongside of'; prefer 'alongside the road.'

rubrics_metrics.name: alot (orthography)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A lot' is two words; 'alot' is incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: already; all ready (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: Already = time; all ready = prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See earlier entry for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: alright (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'all right' (avoid 'alright').

rubrics_metrics.name: altar, alter (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Altar = sacramental table (noun); alter = to change (verb).

rubrics_metrics.name: alternate; alternative (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate can mean substitute or every other; alternative implies another available, usually sounder choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate sense; noun uses correspond. Examples: 'alternate Saturdays' vs 'alternative fuel sources.'

rubrics_metrics.name: altogether; all together (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: See respective entries distinguishing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: amend; emend (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend = change/add to or improve; emend = remove mistakes from a text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'amendment' vs 'emendation' accordingly. Examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: amiable; amicable (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amiable = easy to like (people); amicable = describes relationships/settlements implying goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'an amiable waiter' vs 'an amicable divorce.'

rubrics_metrics.name: amid; among (see between)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to 'between' entry for guidance; choice depends on nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: among (see between)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'between' entry for recommended usages.

rubrics_metrics.name: amount; number (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount with mass nouns; number with count nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'amount of pollution' vs 'a growing number of dissidents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: an (see a)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'a; an' entry for rules based on sound/pronunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: and (sentence starter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a sentence with 'and' is acceptable and often outperforms 'moreover', but does not occur as often as 'but'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comma after 'but' when starting sentences with it; see related entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: and/or (avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'and/or'; often replace with 'and', 'or', or explicit phrasing ('or both') or other constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replace 'take a sleeping pill and/or a warm drink' with 'take a sleeping pill or a warm drink, or both' or other clearer phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: anecdotal (register)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote is a story; 'anecdotal evidence' implies suspect, unverified accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution when implying evidentiary strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: angry (see mad)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to 'mad' entry for nuance and preferred usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: anxious (avoid as eager)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'anxious' as synonym for 'eager'; standard sense is 'worried, nervous, distressed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: anyone; any one (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone (one word) is a singular indefinite pronoun; any one (two words) emphasizes a single individual in a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'anyone would know that' vs 'do you recognize any one of those boys?'

rubrics_metrics.name: anyplace (see anywhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'anywhere' to the informal 'anyplace'.

rubrics_metrics.name: anyway; anyways (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Anyway' is standard; 'anyways' is traditionally dialectal and nonstandard despite recent usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'anyways' in formal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: anywhere; any place (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anywhere preferred for an indefinite location; 'any place' is narrower when meaning 'any location'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid informal 'anyplace'.

rubrics_metrics.name: appertain (see pertain)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'pertain' entry for usage guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: appraise; apprise (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appraise = assess or value; apprise = inform or notify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the jeweler appraised the necklace' vs 'keep me apprised of any developments.'

rubrics_metrics.name: appreciate (senses & concision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three senses: understand fully; increase in value; be grateful. Sense 3 can lead to verbose constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'I would appreciate your letting me know' or simply 'please let me know' over awkward phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: apprise (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'appraise' (entry cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: approve; endorse (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approve implies positive thought or formal sanction; endorse implies positive attitude plus active support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise word depending on passive approval vs active backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: approve (of) (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approve alone connotes official sanction or acceptance; 'approve of' suggests thinking favorably about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the finance committee approved the proposed budget' vs 'she approved of her sister’s new hairstyle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: approximately (see about)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'about; approximately' entry: use 'about' generally and 'approximately' in scientific contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: apt; likely (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apt = fit/suitable or quick to learn; likely = expresses probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'apt' for tendencies/fit ('apt remark') and 'likely' for probability; some objection to 'likely' as synonym for 'probably'.

rubrics_metrics.name: area (usage caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often a nearly meaningless filler ('the area of partnering skills'); delete 'area of' when possible, though in sciences it can be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concision; see 'space' entry for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: as far as (wordiness/nonstandard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often wordy; avoid using 'as far as' in place of 'as for' unless completed with 'is concerned' or 'goes', and even then it is usually wordy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare 'as far as change is concerned' vs 'as for change.'

rubrics_metrics.name: as is (quotation usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In acquisition contexts, 'as is' is framed in quotes to denote acceptance without guarantees; 'on an “as is” basis' is verbose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise phrasing when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: as of yet; as yet (stilted)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As of yet' is stilted and redundant; prefer 'yet', 'still', 'so far'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simpler alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: as per (nonstandard/commercial)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As per' is common in commercial contexts but long considered nonstandard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'as you requested' or 'per your request' rather than 'as per your request.' Avoid 'as per usual' for 'as usual.'

rubrics_metrics.name: assault; battery (legal distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In law, assault = threat causing reasonable fear; battery = intentional physical contact; assault does not require touching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating the terms; legal sense differs from popular usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: assemblage; assembly (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblage = informal collection; assembly = organized group of decision makers, a meeting, or the process of putting parts together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show appropriate senses: 'national assembly' vs 'instructions for assembly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: assent; consent (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assent implies affirmative agreement after consideration; consent implies allowance, possibly grudging acquiescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the term that matches degree of deliberation or formality intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: as such (usage requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As such' requires an antecedent for 'such' and is often misused as 'therefore'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose usage: provide clear antecedent or use 'therefore' where intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: assumption; presumption (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumption = taken without strong evidence; presumption = implies some basis in evidence or experience and can support decision if uncontradicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'your assumption can be tested'; 'the legal presumption of innocence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: assure (see ensure)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'ensure' for guidance on these often-confused words.

rubrics_metrics.name: as to (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best used to begin a sentence where 'on the question of' or 'with regard to' could be used; otherwise prefer 'about' or another preposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'As to those checks, she didn’t know where they came from.'

rubrics_metrics.name: attain; obtain (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attain = accomplish through effort or reach a level/age; obtain = get or gain possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best usage: attain a degree, obtain a diploma; common usage often treats them as synonyms.

rubrics_metrics.name: at the present time; at this time; at present (conciseness)
rubrics_metrics.description: These are turgid substitutes for now, today, currently, or nowadays; 'at present' is least bureaucratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'now' or other concise alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: at the time that; at the time when (simplify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the plain 'when' instead of the verbose phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'when' for clarity and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: auger; augur (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Auger = boring tool; augur = seer or to foretell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related noun 'augury' denotes an indication of future events; 'augurs well' is idiomatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: avenge; revenge (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avenge connotes exaction for a wrong (noun vengeance); revenge connotes inflicting harm out of anger and is more commonly a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'avenge' when referring to exerting justice; 'revenge' as commonly used noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: averse (see adverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'adverse' entry for differences; 'averse' typically relates to people/habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: avocation; vocation (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avocation = hobby; vocation = profession or calling (often religious connotation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'stamp collecting is my avocation' vs 'she had a true vocation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: awhile; a while (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awhile (one word) is adverbial meaning 'for a short time'; 'a while' (two words) is a noun phrase used after prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'let’s stop here awhile' vs 'she worked for a while.'

rubrics_metrics.name: backward(s) (see toward)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'toward' entry for discussion of 'backward' vs 'backwards' and related directional adverbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: bale; bail (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bale = bundle (hay); bail = drain water or post security to get out of jail; also informal 'to leave quickly'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the couple bailed from the party.'

rubrics_metrics.name: based on (legitimate and illegitimate uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate uses: verbal force (base as transitive verb) and adjectival passive (based as participial adjective). Two slipshod uses: adverbial force and prepositional/dangling participle uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'Based on this information, we decided to stay' (dangling). Prefer 'on the basis of this information' or restructure: 'with this information, we decided to stay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: basis (wordiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'foundation'; often appears in 'on a ... basis' constructions that are wordy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute adverbs or state time directly (daily instead of 'on a daily basis'). Plural is 'bases'.

rubrics_metrics.name: bated breath (orthography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct spelling is 'bated breath' (not 'baited breath').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning: anxious or excited waiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: battery (see assault)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'assault' entry for legal distinction between assault and battery.

rubrics_metrics.name: begging the question (logical fallacy and misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally denotes the fallacy of assuming as true what needs proof; often misused to mean 'prompting or inviting a question'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with care to denote the specific logical fallacy, not general prompting.

rubrics_metrics.name: behalf (in behalf of vs on behalf of)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In behalf of' = in the interest of or for the benefit of; 'on behalf of' = acting as agent or representative of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'in behalf of the patient' vs 'on behalf of Mr. Scott.'

rubrics_metrics.name: bemused (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means 'bewildered, distracted, or confused', not a synonym of 'amused'.

rubrics_metrics.name: benevolence; beneficence (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benevolence = disposition to kindness (quality); beneficence = an act of kindness or performance of good deeds (conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term matching abstract quality vs concrete acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: beside; besides (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beside = preposition of position; besides = 'other than' (prep) or 'also' (adverb).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples clarify usage: 'beside the road' vs 'who’s going besides us?' vs 'besides, who wants to know?'

rubrics_metrics.name: between; among; amid (usage distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Between indicates one-to-one relationships (can be used for more than two if relationships are pairwise); among indicates collective/undefined relationships; amid often used with mass nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'amidst' and 'amongst' in American English; use 'between' with plurals when multiple one-to-one relationships are implied; examples provided for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: between you and me (correct pronoun case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct phrasing is 'between you and me' (objects of preposition); 'between you and I' is hypercorrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note on Shakespeare and sociolinguistic context.

rubrics_metrics.name: bi-; semi- (prefix distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bi- generally means 'two' (can be ambiguous); semi- means 'half' or twice-in-period (semiweekly = twice a week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of confusion, writers should be explicit about intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: biannual; semiannual; biennial (clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biannual and semiannual both mean 'twice a year'; biennial means 'once every two years'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid confusion, write 'semiannual' and consider 'once every two years' instead of 'biennial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: billion; trillion (international differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meanings vary historically by country; US: billion = 1,000,000,000; traditional British/Canadian/German: billion = million millions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should remember historical geographic distinctions and possibly clarify magnitude in mixed-audience contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: blatant; flagrant (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blatant = both bad and plain for all to see; flagrant = brazenly open with stronger suggestion of illegality or immorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the word matching degree of brazenness or moral shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: bombastic (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pompously long-winded and self-important but empty of substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not related to temperament; refers to style and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: born; borne (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Born used as adjective or in 'to be born'; borne is past participle of 'bear' and used in compounds (foodborne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a born ruler' vs 'she has borne three children'; compound uses like 'vectorborne'.

rubrics_metrics.name: both-and (correlative conjunctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both-and should frame matching syntactic parts; the elements joined must be parallel in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect: 'She is both a writer and she skis professionally.' Correct: 'She is both a writer and a professional skier.'

rubrics_metrics.name: breach; breech (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breach = gap/violation; breech = lower/back part, especially buttocks or firearm part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'breach of contract' vs 'breech birth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: bring; take (directionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'bring' when action is toward the speaker; 'take' when action is away from the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'bring home the bacon' vs 'take out the trash'; you take your car to the mechanic (away from you).

rubrics_metrics.name: but (sentence starter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning a sentence with 'but' is acceptable and often useful for contrast; avoid placing a comma after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare use with 'and' and see 5.203.

rubrics_metrics.name: by means of (verbosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'By means of' is often verbose; use 'by' or 'with' if they suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: by reason of (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'because' or 'because of' unless part of an established legal phrase ('by reason of insanity').

rubrics_metrics.name: cache; cachet (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cache = stash or computer buffer; cachet = prestige or seal/design; sometimes incorrectly spelled 'caché'.

rubrics_metrics.name: can; could (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can = ability or certainty; could = uncertainty or conditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I can be there in five minutes' vs 'could you stop at the cleaners today?' See 5.146.

rubrics_metrics.name: can; may (permission/possibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can traditionally applies to ability; may suggests possibility or permission. In formal denial of permission, 'may not' is proper; informally use 'can't'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'may not borrow my credit card' vs 'you can’t use the computer tonight.' See 5.146, 5.147.

rubrics_metrics.name: cannon; canon (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannon = artillery weapon; canon = rule/principle/collected works/Christian priest or musical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple senses of 'canon' provided to guide correct word choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: capability (see ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'ability' entry for nuance; 'capability' often refers to power/feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: capacity (see ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'ability' entry for detailed senses (container, power, role, amount).

rubrics_metrics.name: capital; capitol (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital = seat of government, usually a city; capitol = building where a legislature meets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Jefferson City is the capital of Missouri' vs 'the legislature opened its new session in the capitol today.'

rubrics_metrics.name: carat; karat; caret (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carat measures gemstone weight; karat measures gold purity; caret is a manuscript insertion mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory aid: think of 24K gold for karat. Note British spelling differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: career; careen (regional usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In American English 'careen' has taken over verb sense of 'career' (to go full speed); in British English 'career' as a verb persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of regional preferences when choosing verb form.

rubrics_metrics.name: caret (see carat)
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'carat' entry for cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: case (multifaceted word warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'case' can be an overworked filler; it has many legitimate senses (law, medicine, container, argument, grammatical form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbal inflation by using more specific terms when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: cause célèbre (usage/orthography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotes a legal case of public interest; by extension refers to notorious episode/person; retains accents but often not italicized; plural is causes célèbres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use it to mean a beloved 'pet cause.'

rubrics_metrics.name: censer; censor; sensor (spelling distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censer = incense container or person carrying it; censor = person who suppresses content; sensor = device detecting stimulus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for homophones and correct spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: censor; censure (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censor (verb) = remove objectionable material; censure (verb) = criticize strongly or reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the government censors the press' vs 'the House censured the president.'

rubrics_metrics.name: center around (usage advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistists prefer 'center on' or 'revolve around' rather than the illogical 'center around'.

rubrics_metrics.name: certainty; certitude (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certainty = the fact you are sure about; certitude = assurance of being certain (trait applied to people).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terms according to whether you mean the fact/event or a person's assuredness.

rubrics_metrics.name: chair; chairman; chairwoman; chairperson (gender-neutral guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'chair' as the preferred gender-neutral term for the office of authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note and cross-reference to section 5.251-60 for more on gender-neutral forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: childish; childlike (nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Childlike = positive connotation of innocence/eagerness; childish = pejorative, immaturity/silliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'childlike' to praise innocence, 'childish' to criticize immaturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: chord; cord (difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chord = musical harmony or geometric line; cord = thick string/nerve/wire or measurement of firewood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided to select correct homophone.

rubrics_metrics.name: circumstances; in the circumstances / under the circumstances (preference)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In the circumstances' and 'under the circumstances' are both acceptable; 'under' is more common in American English, 'in' predominates in British English.
